A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same NRF research work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

before.justification: V1 reports original NSD encoding and cross-subject adaptation experiments, coordinate perturbations, and architectural ablations.

after.justification: V2 retains those experiments and adds subject-level analyses, statistical results, and a high-resolution querying demonstration.

M1.justification: Sections 3.1–3.2 and the architecture appendices retain the same CLIP features, Fourier coordinate encoding, eight-layer MLP, training loss, fine-tuning procedure, and voxelwise regression ensemble. Higher-resolution querying exercises the existing method.

E1.justification: NSD, the visual encoding task, and the principal four-subject evaluation remain unchanged. V2 adds a qualitative non-native-grid scenario: Subject 1 predictions queried at 0.5 mm alongside measured responses acquired at 1.8 mm (Appendix A.8, Figure 6).

E2.justification: Linear regression, fWRF, and MindSimulator remain the main comparison methods. The scratch, fine-tuned base-model, averaging, and regression-ensemble comparisons are also retained. Newly discussed transformer encoders and cross-subject decoders are cited without being added to the experiments.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 changes the stated testing metric from R-squared to Pearson correlation, consistent with the metrics already reported in v1; this does not establish a rerun. Appendix A.8 introduces the explicit 0.5 mm querying setting. Existing splits, training settings, and reconstruction metrics are retained.

E4.justification: V2 adds per-subject voxel-accuracy distribution summaries in Figure 5 and a case study demonstrating querying beyond the acquisition grid in Figure 6. Existing coordinate perturbations, ensemble comparisons, fine-tuning ablations, and MLP depth/width ablations remain; the latter move from v1 Tables 4–6 to v2 Tables 21–23.

E5.justification: Beyond v1's cross-subject SEM in Figure 2, v2 adds 10,000 sign-flip permutation tests, BH-FDR correction, Cohen's d, correlation significance tests, and significant-voxel fractions (Appendix A.5). Tables 5 and 20 also provide SEM for existing evaluations. These are substantial new statistical reporting practices; increased training-run or seed counts are not documented.

E6.justification: All nine original tables retain their numerical entries after matching renumbering. V2 nevertheless adds substantial subject-level results, statistical outcomes, adaptation summaries, and fine-grid predictions. Figure 4 exchanges the curve assignments between EBA and V1. Some new entries conflict with retained results: Table 4 reports Subject 7's full-data correlation as 0.278, whereas Table 2 retains 0.269; this is not an established performance gain.

T1.justification: The continuous response formulation, Fourier encoding, loss expression, and ensemble equations are unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs, and v2 adds no formal derivation.

C1.justification: The central claims about continuous anatomical encoding, data efficiency, and cross-subject transfer remain. The introduction locally narrows the digital-twin aspiration from the brain to the human visual system and replaces its explicit first-model characterization with a novel framework; the abstract and conclusion retain broader wording.

C2.justification: Appendix A.3 strengthens the existing decoder-bias caveat by declaring semantic metrics diagnostic and voxel-level metrics the exclusive basis for core comparisons. Section 5.4 adds the interpretation that ensembling combines specialized knowledge from source subjects rather than merely reducing noise.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code/project link and a reproducibility statement promising release of preprocessed data, code, and model parameters. It also clarifies median-based aggregation and supplies subject-specific voxel counts. Existing implementation details remain unchanged; the PDFs do not establish whether the linked resources are available.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands positioning against transformer encoders, spatial-prior models, cross-subject decoders, and cortical semantic mapping, adding works including Adeli et al. (2025), MindBridge, and MindLLM. It distinguishes continuous encoding from coordinate-assisted discrete decoding and post-hoc spatial visualization, and qualifies the related-work novelty claim as one of the first.

P1.justification: V2 polishes introduction/results prose, clarifies the decoding pipeline, and reorganizes the appendices with a contents list, relocated ablations and LLM disclosure, and separate ethics/reproducibility statements. The main section sequence and most method exposition remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds extensive statistical and subject-level table displays and Figures 5–6, substantially reorganizing the appendix presentation. Figure 4 is redrawn with common vertical scales, and captions clarify aggregation. Table 19 repeats the existing Subject 7 adaptation results rather than displaying a new experiment.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1's mainly aggregated reporting, v2 makes subject variation and statistical evidence inspectable, clarifies metric interpretation, and better situates the contribution. These transparency gains are limited by inconsistencies: Appendix A.5 claims uniformly significant superiority despite nonsignificant and negative effects in Table 6, and new Table 4 conflicts with retained Table 2 for Subject 7. Figure 6 demonstrates finer querying without validating fine-scale accuracy. The net gain is therefore in reporting and context, with stronger empirical reliability still unresolved.
